content.intro: This lesson covers Function Signatures and Type Checking. It sits in Module 5, Functions, Scope, and Program Flow, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Function Signatures and Type Checking matters when you work with language foundations. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Function Signatures and Type Checking is one building block of this area: Design functions with explicit inputs, outputs, scope, and control flow. Start with the smallest example, identify the inputs and assumptions, and check the edge cases before using the technique in a larger program.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Function Signatures and Type Checking, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Functions make inputs and outputs explicit. Keep them small enough to test and prefer returning a Result when callers can reasonably recover from a failure.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Function Signatures and Type Checking guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
